title: Fallout shelter basics: where to shelter from radioactive fallout, and what shields you
asks: where is the best place to shelter from fallout
what makes a good fallout shelter
is my basement a good fallout shelter
is a car safe from fallout
does a wood house protect from radiation
how much dirt or concrete stops fallout radiation
how long do i have to stay in a fallout shelter
do i need to seal the windows against fallout
fallout expected here, which part of the building do we use, over
answer: The best protection from fallout radiation is underground (basements, subway tunnels, underground parking garages) or in the center of a large, heavy building.
Inside, stay away from windows, corners, doors, outside walls and the roof.
An adequate shelter reduces the radiation dose by a factor of 10 or more. Examples: basements; the centers of large, multi-story structures; parking garages; tunnels.
Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters: they lack dense shielding material. Single-story wood-frame houses without basements also provide only limited shielding.

Any shelter is better than being outside for extended periods of time. A smaller wood or steel frame house does not usually provide adequate protection above ground, but it is still far better than being outside. Thicker-walled masonry buildings and residential basements generally provide adequate protection.

Good shielding materials are concrete, brick, stone and earth. Wood, drywall and thin sheet metal provide minimal shielding, but many layers of them can also provide adequate protection, for example a central room with many walls in between.
To protect against fallout radiation: reduce the time spent in radioactive areas, increase your distance from the fallout, and use dense materials (concrete, brick or earth) as shielding.
A shelter does not need to be airtight. A building with minor damage can be used if it is structurally sound, and even buildings with broken windows can provide adequate protection.
Close windows and doors to minimize the outdoor air drawn into the building, but maintain enough ventilation for adequate indoor air quality.

A 3-foot thickness of earth, or a 2-foot thickness of concrete, is an effective barrier: it absorbs about 99.9% of the gamma rays from fallout. About 3.6 inches (9 centimeters) of packed earth reduces by half the radiation dose that passes through it.
For good protection you must be shielded overhead and on all sides.
It is best to be in the shelter when the fallout arrives.

How long to stay: FEMA's Are You Ready guide says to stay inside for 24 hours unless local authorities provide other instructions. FEMA's planning guidance says 12 to 24 hours unless provided additional guidance, and its template alert message says at least 24 hours.

FEMA's planning guidance also says that, where possible, people should stay in an adequate shelter for the first 24 hours following detonation, and that optimal shelter stay times can range from a few hours to several days, depending on the local fallout dose rate and on the radiation dose that would be received during evacuation.

A much longer figure comes from a different situation: the Oak Ridge civil-defense manual Nuclear War Survival Skills, published in 1979 and written for an all-out nuclear attack, says that within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them, or could work outside for an increasing number of hours each day. Its exceptions are areas of extremely heavy fallout, such as downwind from important targets attacked with many weapons.
The same manual says that to know when to come out safely, shelter occupants need a reliable fallout meter, or information based on measurements made nearby with a reliable instrument.
warnings: In the first few hours, lethal radiation levels may be present even tens of miles from ground zero and where fallout is not apparent. The hazard decreases significantly over time.
Immediate threats to life take priority: leaving the shelter may be warranted in the event of fire, building collapse or a medical emergency.

quotes.text: The best radiation protection is underground (e.g., basements, subway tunnels, underground parking garages) or in the center of large, heavy buildings.

The best initial action following a nuclear explosion is moving to and remaining within an accessible, adequate shelter away from windows, corners, doors, and outside walls. Individuals should plan to remain sheltered for at least 12‒24 hours.

Stay away from the outer walls and roof. This will help provide protection from the blast, heat, and radiation of the detonation. Stay inside for 24 hours unless local authorities provide other instructions.

Adequate shelters reduce radiation doses by a factor of 10 or more and examples include basements; centers of large, multi-story structures; parking garages, and tunnels. Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters because they lack dense shielding material. Good shielding materials include concrete, brick, stone, and earth. Wood, drywall, and thin sheet metal provide minimal shielding. However, many layers of minimal shielding materials can also provide adequate protection (e.g., central rooms with many intervening drywalls). Structures do not need to be airtight to protect against fallout radiation, so buildings with minor damage can be used as shelters if they are structurally sound.
Vehicles and single-story wood frame houses without basements provide limited shielding and should not be considered adequate shelter.
It is best to be in a shelter when fallout arrives. Any shelter is better than being outside for extended periods of time. Stay Inside for 12–24 hours, unless provided additional guidance.

Prepare to stay inside for at least 24 hours unless officials provide other instructions, or your building is threatened by fire or collapse. Follow instructions from officials – this can save your life.

Optimal shelter stay times can range from a few hours to several days and depend both on the local fallout dose rate and the radiation dose incurred during evacuation. Where possible, individuals should stay in an adequate shelter for the first 24 hours following detonation to prevent exposure to high levels of radiation.

Smaller single-family homes, particularly wood/steel frame houses, do not usually provide adequate protection above ground, though is still far better than being outside. Thickerwalled masonry buildings and residential basements generally provide adequate protection.
To protect against radiation fallout: Reduce time spent in radioactive areas Increase distance from source of radiation (fallout) Use dense materials (e.g., concrete, brick, or earth) as shielding

Fallout exposure can be effectively minimized by taking shelter in a protective structure. The outdoor radiation hazard from fallout (often referred to as the “ground shine dose”) is typically orders of magnitude more hazardous than internal exposure concerns resulting from inhalation or ingestion of radioactive material. Even buildings with broken windows can provide adequate protection from ground shine dose.
Close windows and doors to minimize the amount of outdoor air being drawn into the building. Make sure to maintain enough ventilation to ensure adequate indoor air quality.
The 3-foot thickness of earth shown (or a 2-foot thickness of concrete) will provide an effective barrier, attenuating (absorbing) about 99.9% of all gamma rays from fallout.
Each of the layers shown is one halving-thickness of packed earth-about 3.6 inches (9 centimeters).
A halvingthickness is the thickness of a material which reduces by half the dose of radiation that passes through it.
For good protection he must be protected overhead and on all sides by barrier shielding.
NUCLEAR WAR SURVIVAL SKILLS Cresson H. Kearny
Date Published-September 1979
These instructions have been improved repeatedly by Oak Ridge National Laboratory civil defense researchers over a period of eight years and are the heart of this book.

Even if our country remained unprepared and were to be subjected to an all-out nuclear attack, many millions of Americans would survive and be in favorable conditions to live through difficult post-attack years.

Within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them, or could work outside the shelters for an increasing number of hours each day. Exceptions would be in areas of extremely heavy fallout such as might occur downwind from important targets attacked with many weapons, especially missile sites and very large cities. To know when to come out safely, occupants either would need a reliable fallout meter to measure the changing radiation dangers, or must receive information based on measurements made nearby with a reliable instrument.

In the first few hours, lethal radiation levels may be present―even in areas tens of miles from ground zero and/or where fallout is not apparent. The hazard of the fallout radiation will decrease significantly over time, enabling safer evacuations.
As with all guidance, immediate threats to life take priority, so evacuation may be warranted in the event of fire, building collapse, or medical emergencies.

conflict: How long to stay sheltered: the sources describe different scenarios and give different times. FEMA (guidance for the response to a nuclear detonation): Are You Ready (2020) 'Stay inside for 24 hours unless local authorities provide other instructions'; Planning Guidance (2022) 'at least 12-24 hours'; First 72 Hours (2023) 'at least the first 24 hours'. ORNL-5037 (1979, all-out attack): 'Within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them', longer in areas of extremely heavy fallout. The revised card shows the three FEMA figures in the same words as the nuclear-detonation-first-actions card (24 hours unless local authorities provide other instructions; 12 to 24 hours unless provided additional guidance; at least 24 hours in the template alert message), adds the Planning Guidance lines 'Where possible, individuals should stay in an adequate shelter for the first 24 hours following detonation' and 'Optimal shelter stay times can range from a few hours to several days and depend both on the local fallout dose rate and the radiation dose incurred during evacuation', and labels the ORNL figure as coming from a civil-defense manual published in 1979 and written for an all-out nuclear attack ('Even if our country... were to be subjected to an all-out nuclear attack'; exceptions 'downwind from important targets attacked with many weapons'). Note for the owner: 'its template alert message', wording copied from the nuclear-detonation card, is the Wireless Emergency Alert template in FEMA's First 72 Hours guide (2023), not in the Planning Guidance, so 'its' is exact only if read as FEMA's; if the owner wants the document named, both cards should be changed together. The card does not call FEMA's guidance 'single detonation' because the 2022 Planning Guidance says it also 'addresses an expanded range of threat scenarios, including nation-state threats'. Also, on vehicles: FEMA (2022) says 'Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters because they lack dense shielding material'; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003), written for responders near a radiation source, says 'If possible, use clothing, vehicles, equipment, containers or natural barriers like hills, trees, and rocks to protect yourself from radiation exposure', adding that they 'may not provide adequate shielding'. The card gives only FEMA's fallout-shelter statement.

review.notes: previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Fail. Drafter flag verdict (durations): the card silently picks the shortest FEMA figure. It shows only 'at least 12 to 24 hours' (Planning Guidance 2022), while the nuclear-detonation card shows 24 h (Are You Ready), 12-24 h (Planning Guidance) and at least 24 h (First 72 Hours) side by side, and the Planning Guidance itself also says 'Where possible, individuals should stay in an adequate shelter for the first 24 hours following detonation' and 'Optimal shelter stay times can range from a few hours to several days and depend both on the local fallout dose rate and the radiation dose incurred during evacuation.' A reader of this card could leave at 12 hours. Fix: give the same FEMA figures as the nuclear-detonation card (keep the two cards' wording identical), with 'unless officials give other instructions', and add the 'few hours to several days, depending on the local fallout dose rate' line. ORNL 'within two weeks': keep, but say it comes from a 1979 civil-defence manual written for an all-out attack with many weapons, so it is not read as contradicting FEMA's single-detonation guidance. Rest verified: underground or centre of a large heavy building; away from windows, corners, doors, outer walls and roof; factor of 10; vehicles and single-story wood-frame houses inadequate; any shelter better than outside; dense materials and many layers; not airtight, broken windows, close windows but keep ventilation; 3 ft earth / 2 ft concrete about 99.9 percent, 3.6-in halving thickness; overhead and all sides; be inside before fallout arrives; fallout meter; lethal levels tens of miles out; life threats take priority. HHS's vehicle line is correctly left out (responder context).
